implies that that affine subspaces on the left contains
0
, thus the affine shift on the left must be in the linear space on the right:

\begin{bmatrix}x\end{bmatrix}\in\ker\begin{bmatrix}[c|c]I&iJ_{k}\end{bmatrix}

so that

x=\begin{bmatrix}0\\
0\\
0\\
x_{4}\end{bmatrix}

Now that the affine shift has been taken care of we end up with the equality:

\ker\begin{bmatrix}[cc|cc]I&0&iJ_{r}&0\\
0&0&0&I\end{bmatrix}S=\ker\begin{bmatrix}[cc|cc]I&0&iI_{k}&0\\
0&0&0&I\end{bmatrix}

For a real linear symplectomorphism
S
. In other words, such that there exists real matrices
A,B,C,D,X
and
Y
, with
X+iY
invertible and

\begin{bmatrix}A&B\\
C&D\end{bmatrix}

a symplectomorphism, such that:

\begin{bmatrix}[c|c]I&iJ_{r}\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}A&B\\
C&D\end{bmatrix}=\left(X+iY\right)\begin{bmatrix}[c|c]I&iJ_{k}\end{bmatrix}

This gives:

\begin{bmatrix}[c|c]A+iJ_{r}C&B+iJ_{r}D\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}[c|c]X+iY&-Y\Phi+iX\Phi\end{bmatrix}

and then by identifying the real and imaginary parts:

\begin{cases}A=X\\
J_{r}C=Y\\
B=-YI_{k}\\
J_{r}D=XI_{k}\end{cases}

we can eliminate
X
and
Y
:

\begin{cases}B=-J_{r}CI_{k}\\
J_{r}D=AI_{k}\end{cases}

To this we can furthermore add the symplectic condition giving:

\begin{cases}B=-J_{r}CJ_{k}\\
J_{r}D=AJ_{k}\\
B^{\mathsf{T}}D=D^{\mathsf{T}}B\\
A^{\mathsf{T}}C=C^{\mathsf{T}}A\\
I=A^{\mathsf{T}}D-C^{\mathsf{T}}B\end{cases}

Notice that the third equation follows from the others:

B^{\mathsf{T}}D=-J_{k}C^{\mathsf{T}}J_{r}D=-J_{k}C^{\mathsf{T}}AJ_{k}=-J_{k}A^{\mathsf{T}}CJ_{k}=-D^{\mathsf{T}}J_{r}CJ_{k}=-D^{\mathsf{T}}B.

We can now eliminate
B
and get:

\begin{cases}J_{r}D=AJ_{k}\\
A^{\mathsf{T}}C=C^{\mathsf{T}}A\\
I=A^{\mathsf{T}}D+C^{\mathsf{T}}J_{r}CJ_{k}\end{cases}

We can now divide our matrices in blocks:

A\coloneqq\begin{bmatrix}A_{1}&A_{2}\\
A_{3}&A_{4}\end{bmatrix}\qquad C\coloneqq\begin{bmatrix}C_{1}&C_{2}\\
C_{3}&C_{4}\end{bmatrix}\qquad D\coloneqq\begin{bmatrix}D_{1}&D_{2}\\
D_{3}&D_{4}\end{bmatrix}

The first constraint then gives:

\begin{bmatrix}I&0\\
0&0\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}D_{1}&D_{2}\\
D_{3}&D_{4}\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}A_{1}&A_{2}\\
A_{3}&A_{4}\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}I&0\\
0&0\end{bmatrix}

Implying that
D_{2}=0
,
A_{3}=0
, and
A_{1}=D_{1}
. The third constraint gives:

\begin{bmatrix}I&0\\
0&I\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}A_{1}^{\mathsf{T}}&0\\
A_{2}^{\mathsf{T}}&A_{4}^{\mathsf{T}}\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}A_{1}&0\\
D_{3}&D_{4}\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}C_{1}^{\mathsf{T}}&C_{3}^{\mathsf{T}}\\
C_{2}^{\mathsf{T}}&C_{4}^{\mathsf{T}}\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}I&0\\
0&0\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}C_{1}&C_{2}\\
C_{3}&C_{4}\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}I&0\\
0&0\end{bmatrix}

\begin{bmatrix}I&0\\
0&I\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}A_{1}^{\mathsf{T}}A_{1}&0\\
A_{2}^{\mathsf{T}}A_{1}+A_{4}^{\mathsf{T}}D_{3}&A_{4}^{\mathsf{T}}D_{4}\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}C_{1}^{\mathsf{T}}C_{1}&0\\
C_{2}^{\mathsf{T}}C_{1}&0\end{bmatrix}

This implies that
A_{4}^{\mathsf{T}}D_{4}=I
, so the
(n-r)\times(n-k)
matrix
D_{4}
is injective. Therefore,
(n-k)\leqslant(n-r)
, and thus
r\leqslant k
. Since the role of
k
and
r
is symmetric up to replacing
S
by its inverse, we finally get that
r=k
, and that
A_{4}^{\mathsf{T}}
is invertible. We can now eliminate
D_{4}=A_{4}^{-\mathsf{T}}
and reformulate the third constraint as:

\begin{cases}I=A_{1}^{\mathsf{T}}A_{1}+C_{1}^{\mathsf{T}}C_{1}\\
D_{3}=-A_{4}^{-\mathsf{T}}A_{2}^{\mathsf{T}}A_{1}-A_{4}^{-\mathsf{T}}C_{2}^{\mathsf{T}}C_{1}\\
\end{cases}

Allowing to eliminate
D_{3}
. The second constraint gives us:

\begin{bmatrix}A_{1}^{\mathsf{T}}&0\\
A_{2}^{\mathsf{T}}&A_{4}^{\mathsf{T}}\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}C_{1}&C_{2}\\
C_{3}&C_{4}\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}C_{1}^{\mathsf{T}}&C_{3}^{\mathsf{T}}\\
C_{2}^{\mathsf{T}}&C_{4}^{\mathsf{T}}\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}A_{1}&A_{2}\\
0&A_{4}\end{bmatrix}

In other words:

\begin{cases}A_{1}^{\mathsf{T}}C_{1}=C_{1}^{\mathsf{T}}A_{1}\\
A_{2}^{\mathsf{T}}C_{1}+A_{4}^{\mathsf{T}}C_{3}=C_{2}^{\mathsf{T}}A_{1}\\
A_{2}^{\mathsf{T}}C_{2}+A_{4}^{\mathsf{T}}C_{4}=C_{2}^{\mathsf{T}}A_{2}+C_{4}^{\mathsf{T}}A_{4}\\
\end{cases}

We can thus eliminate
C_{3}=A_{4}^{-\mathsf{T}}C_{2}^{\mathsf{T}}A_{1}-A_{4}^{-\mathsf{T}}A_{2}^{\mathsf{T}}C_{1}
.

If we gather the constraints we have so far, we have only
A_{1}
,
A_{2}
,
A_{4}
,
C_{1}
,
C_{2}
and
C_{4}
as degree of freedom satisfying:

\begin{cases}I=A_{1}^{\mathsf{T}}A_{1}+C_{1}^{\mathsf{T}}C_{1}\\
A_{1}^{\mathsf{T}}C_{1}=C_{1}^{\mathsf{T}}A_{1}\\
A_{2}^{\mathsf{T}}C_{2}+A_{4}^{\mathsf{T}}C_{4}=C_{2}^{\mathsf{T}}A_{2}+C_{4}^{\mathsf{T}}A_{4}\end{cases}

We get the following symplectomorphism:

\begin{bmatrix}A_{1}&A_{2}&-C_{1}&0\\
0&A_{4}&0&0\\
C_{1}&C_{2}&A_{1}&0\\
A_{4}^{-\mathsf{T}}C_{2}^{\mathsf{T}}A_{1}-A_{4}^{-\mathsf{T}}A_{2}^{\mathsf{T}}C_{1}&C_{4}&-A_{4}^{-\mathsf{T}}A_{2}^{\mathsf{T}}A_{1}-A_{4}^{-\mathsf{T}}C_{2}^{\mathsf{T}}C_{1}&A_{4}^{-\mathsf{T}}\end{bmatrix}

We can now decompose it. First
A_{4}\in\operatorname{Gl}_{n-r}(\mathbb{R})
only acts on the lower part:

\begin{bmatrix}I&0&0&0\\
0&A_{4}&0&0\\
0&0&I&0\\
0&0&0&A_{4}^{-\mathsf{T}}\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}A_{1}&A_{2}&-C_{1}&0\\
0&I&0&0\\
C_{1}&C_{2}&A_{1}&0\\
C_{2}^{\mathsf{T}}A_{1}-A_{2}^{\mathsf{T}}C_{1}&A_{4}^{\mathsf{T}}C_{4}&-A_{2}^{\mathsf{T}}A_{1}-C_{2}^{\mathsf{T}}C_{1}&I\end{bmatrix}

Then, we can see the symplectic rotation

\begin{bmatrix}A_{1}&-C_{1}\\
C_{1}&A_{1}\end{bmatrix}

acting on the upper part:

\begin{bmatrix}I&0&0&0\\
0&A_{4}&0&0\\
0&0&I&0\\
0&0&0&A_{4}^{-\mathsf{T}}\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}I&A_{2}&0&0\\
0&I&0&0\\
0&C_{2}&I&0\\
C_{2}^{\mathsf{T}}&A_{4}^{\mathsf{T}}C_{4}&-A_{2}^{\mathsf{T}}&I\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}A_{1}&0&-C_{1}&0\\
0&I&0&0\\
C_{1}&0&A_{1}&0\\
0&0&0&I\end{bmatrix}

Finally, denoting
\beta\coloneqq A_{4}^{\mathsf{T}}C_{4}+A_{2}^{\mathsf{T}}C_{2}
, we know that
\beta
is symmetric, thus we end up with a symplectomorphism of the form:

\begin{bmatrix}I&0&0&0\\
0&A_{4}&0&0\\
0&0&I&0\\
0&0&0&A_{4}^{-\mathsf{T}}\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}I&A_{2}&0&0\\
0&I&0&0\\
0&0&I&0\\
0&0&-A_{2}^{\mathsf{T}}&I\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}I&0&0&0\\
0&I&0&0\\
0&C_{2}&I&0\\
C_{2}^{\mathsf{T}}&\beta&0&I\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}A_{1}&0&-C_{1}&0\\
0&I&0&0\\
C_{1}&0&A_{1}&0\\
0&0&0&I\end{bmatrix}

Then in
\mathsf{GSA}_{\mathbb{R}}
:

=
S
U
C_{2}
A_{4}
\vec{x},\beta
A_{2}

Where
U
is a symplectic rotation.
∎

Proof of theorem
38
.

(0,i)
